title.rendered: Two Democracies, One Uncertain Future

content.rendered: What holds a democracy together when its citizens disagree about their identities, values, and vision for the future? In the wake of consequential elections in the United States and Israel, Congresswoman Haley Stevens and Tal Becker of the Shalom Hartman Institute explore the responsibilities of democratic leadership, the challenges of governing amid political division, and what it takes to sustain a sense of shared national purpose. Drawing on their different experiences, they consider how leaders can navigate competing values, build trust across differences, and sustain democratic commitments at home and strong partnerships abroad.

title.rendered: James Loeffler: Exceptional Hatred

content.rendered:
How has antisemitism shaped American life, and what makes this moment different? Join Hartman Senior Fellow at the Kogod Research Center, historian James Loeffler, for a conversation about antisemitism, free speech and the challenges facing American democracy. Drawing on Loeffler’s new book, Exceptional Hatred: Antisemitism and the Fight over Free Speech in Modern America, the evening will explore why Jews and Israel so often stand at the center of debates over free expression, and how we can confront hatred while protecting fundamental freedoms. We will consider what history reveals about the fragility and resilience of liberal democracy, and where we might go from here.

Join us for an evening of conversation with esteemed scholar and author James Loeffler as he discusses his new book Exceptional Hatred: Antisemitism and the Fight Over Free Speech in Modern America.

title.rendered: Hartman Leadership Conference – DC

content.rendered:
Led by Hartman’s premier faculty, the Hartman Leadership Conference is an immersive weekend of learning that brings together communal lay leaders, philanthropists, and learners from across North America to explore foundational Jewish ideas and the central dilemmas shaping contemporary Jewish life.

Through rigorous text study, meaningful conversation, and shared community, participants will engage with Hartman scholars and one another around the questions facing the Jewish people today.

title.rendered: Book Talk – Exceptional Hatred: Antisemitism and Free Speech in America, Past and Present

content.rendered:
How has antisemitism shaped American life, and what makes this moment different? Join historian James Loeffler and The New Yorker staff writer Emma Green for a conversation about antisemitism, free speech, and the challenges facing American democracy. Drawing on Loeffler’s new book, they will explore why Jews and Israel so often stand at the center of debates over free expression — and how we can confront hatred while protecting fundamental freedoms. Together, they will consider what history reveals about the fragility and resilience of liberal democracy, and where we might go from here.

James Loeffler is the Felix Posen Professor in Modern Jewish History at Johns Hopkins University, where he also directs the Jewish Studies Program. His research explores Jewish history, antisemitism, free speech, and human rights. His books include Exceptional Hatred: Antisemitism and the Fight over Free Speech in Modern America and the award-winning Rooted Cosmopolitans: Jews and Human Rights in the Twentieth Century.

Emma Green covers education and academia as a staff writer for The New Yorker. Previously, she reported on religion and politics for The Atlantic, where she also served as managing editor. Her honors include the George W. Hunt, S.J., Prize and the Religion News Association’s Supple Award for feature writing.

title.rendered: Rebuilding Trust After Rupture

content.rendered:
What does it take to remain committed to a country after trust has been broken? A classical midrash and a short story by Wallace Stegner offer new ways to think about anger, despair, commitment, and connection. In this final session, we will explore how human relationships endure moments of rupture without losing all hope of repair, and what they can teach us about rebuilding trust in a country that has disappointed us.

___________________________________________________________________________

What does it mean to love a country when it disappoints us? In this three-part online series, How to Love a Country After Disappointment, Deborah Barer and Tamara Mann Tweel will explore the complex relationship between despair and patriotism, loyalty and critique, and love and disappointment. Drawing on sources ranging from rabbinic literature to canonical American texts and short stories, we will reckon with how to re-form national attachments after moments of lost faith or rupture. Together, we will consider how individuals and communities remain connected to a country whose actions fall short of their ideals. Bringing Jewish and American voices into conversation, we will explore how our religious and national traditions can help us better think about patriotism, disappointment, and civic responsibility at this moment in American Jewish life.

These three sessions form a series, but participants may attend individual classes even if they cannot attend all three. Register once to receive the Zoom links for each session.

title.rendered: Dealing with Rupture After the Loss of a Dream

content.rendered:
This session explores rupture and disappointment as perennial themes in a national project. It puts classic American songs, like Paul Simon’s American Tune, into conversation with classical Jewish texts, one expressing disappointment with the Second Temple when it was built, and the other navigating despair after it fell. Both the history of the song and these classical texts offer approaches to rebuilding commitment after moments of shattering loss.

title.rendered: Loving a Country that Doesn’t Love You Back

content.rendered:
This session places classical Jewish texts in conversation with a short story by Ralph Ellison to explore essential civic themes like commitment and rejection. Intertwining stories of both racial and theological rejection, the class examines how moments of transcendence can re-orient us towards the beauty and promise of a collective national project, even in moments of difficulty and despair.

title.rendered: After the Vote: What Israel’s Election Means Now

content.rendered:
Israelis will cast their ballots on October 27. Join Hartman Senior Fellow Tal Becker and journalist Abigail Pogrebin in-person on election night for a timely conversation about what the results might reveal about Israel’s future.

Together, they will look beyond the headlines and electoral arithmetic to consider the deeper questions emerging from the vote: What does this election tell us about Israeli society and its competing visions for the country’s future? What might the results mean for Israel’s democracy, its political institutions, and its relationships with the Jewish world and the international community? And in a moment when the stakes feel especially high, how should we understand what Israelis have just said at the ballot box?

This gathering will provide a unique opportunity to reflect on the deeper political and societal currents defining Israel’s future.

title.rendered: Israel’s 2026 Election

content.rendered:
Israel’s next election will be the first national election after October 7 and the wars that followed. More than a contest between parties, it is likely to become a referendum on Israel’s democratic character, the balance between security and civil society, the role of religion and nationalism in public life, and the future of Jewish-Arab relations inside Israel.

This talk will examine how Israel’s internal questions – trust in state institutions, Ultra-Orthodox enlistment, Arab-Palestinian citizenship, religion and state, and the meaning of democratic governance after trauma – are inseparable from Israel’s regional future, its relationship with the international community, and the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

Masua Sagiv is a Senior Faculty member of the Shalom Hartman Institute and the academic advisor of its Center for Shared Society, as well as a senior fellow at the Helen Diller Institute, U.C. Berkeley.

Co-sponsored by UBC Diamond Chair in Jewish Law and Ethics, the Shalom Hartman Institute of Canada and Temple Sholom.

Free to attend. Registration required.

title.rendered: Jewish Storytelling at a Time of Extremism

content.rendered:
Israel’s upcoming elections will affect the political standing of Jewish extremist movements. How can understanding the past help us navigate some of the most urgent questions these movements pose?  What responsibilities do writers bear when documenting painful personal and communal histories and contested narratives?

Join acclaimed authors Yossi Klein Halevi and Yardena Schwartz in conversation with Claire E. Sufrin, Hartman’s VP of Research and Publication, for a timely exploration of the history of Jewish extremism in Israel and the involvement of American-born leaders in its growth and development. Drawing on Halevi’s Memoirs of a Jewish Extremist (1995) and Schwartz’s Ghosts of a Holy War: The 1929 Massacre in Palestine That Ignited the Arab-Israeli Conflict, recently released in paperback, the conversation will trace the historical, religious, and political currents that shaped extremist movements and examine their implications for today. They will reflect on how their own reporting, research, and personal experiences have informed their understanding of extremism, identity, and peoplehood.

Zoom link to be received following registration

title.rendered: Israel Votes: A Defining Moment for Israel and Jewish Peoplehood

content.rendered:
As Israelis prepare to head to the polls, the stakes extend far beyond the outcome of a single election. The questions facing Israel today touch on its democracy, security, identity, and social cohesion, raising fundamental issues that will shape the future of the Jewish state for years to come.

Join Donniel Hartman, President of the Shalom Hartman Institute, for a timely exploration of the questions, challenges, and opportunities facing Israel as voters prepare to shape the country’s next chapter. How might the election influence Israel’s future direction? What values, aspirations, and tensions are shaping Israeli society? And as Israel’s choices reverberate far beyond its borders, what could this moment mean for Jewish peoplehood and the relationship between Israel and Jewish communities in Canada and around the world?

Following his remarks, Donniel Hartman will join Rabbi Steven Wernick for a conversation exploring what is at stake in this pivotal moment.

title.rendered: The Road to the Israeli Elections

content.rendered: Israel’s political arena is as dynamic and consequential as ever as the march towards the October 27 election is in full swing. This virtual briefing will examine the forces driving the upcoming election, the leadership of Israel’s political parties, and the issues that are fueling voter blocs. Join Tani Frank, Director of The Judaism and State Policy Center at the Shalom Hartman Institute in Israel in conversation with Masua Sagiv, Senior Faculty member of the Shalom Hartman Institute in Israel as they unpack the complexities of Israel’s political landscape in this moment.

title.rendered: Past as Prologue: Rethinking Antisemitism Today

content.rendered:
Join us for an evening with Flora Cassen, Hartman Senior Fellow and Lavine Family Director of the Brandeis Center for Jewish Studies and the Sarnat Center for the Study of Anti-Jewishness, celebrating her new book, Stained Glass: A Reflective History of Antisemitism.

Blending memoir, family history, and historical analysis, Cassen traces Jewish life in Europe from the medieval period through the Holocaust and into the present, examining how enduring myths and prejudices continue to shape Jewish experience. Drawing on her upbringing in Antwerp and her family’s history, the book offers a deeply personal and rigorous exploration of antisemitism across time and place.

Cassen will be in conversation with Arno Rosenfeld, a reporter at the Forward and author of the Antisemitism Decoded newsletter. Together, they will explore the historical roots and contemporary realities of antisemitism, followed by time for community conversation and reflection.

Presented in partnership with

title.rendered: War, Destiny, and Responsibility: Israel and the Future of Jewish Peoplehood

content.rendered:
Israel and the Jewish people are living through one of the most consequential and uncertain periods in recent history. What began in the aftermath of October 7 has evolved into a broader and more volatile regional conflict, including direct confrontation with Iran, reshaping the security landscape and reverberating across Jewish communities worldwide.

Join Zack Bodner, President and CEO of the Oshman Family JCC, as he interviews acclaimed author and Shalom Hartman Institute Senior Fellow Yossi Klein Halevi in a wide-ranging public conversation about how this historic moment is transforming Israeli society and redefining the meaning of Jewish peoplehood. Together they will explore questions of resilience, moral responsibility, solidarity and the evolving relationship between Israel and Jews around the world.

This timely program offers an opportunity to step back from daily headlines and engage thoughtfully with the deeper challenges and possibilities shaping Jewish life in the months and years ahead.

excerpt.rendered: Yossi Klein Halevi, Shalom Hartman Institute Senior Fellow, and Zack Bodner, OFJCC President and CEO discuss how this historic moment is redefining the meaning of Jewish peoplehood.

title.rendered: Jewish America at 250: Values, Vision, and the Next Era

content.rendered:
As the United States approaches its 250th anniversary, American Jews find themselves at a pivotal crossroads. This moment—marked by cultural upheaval, rising antisemitism, shifting political landscapes, and evolving ties to Israel—presents both profound challenges and extraordinary opportunities.

Join Yehuda Kurtzer, President of the Shalom Hartman Institute in conversation with Jeffrey Goldberg, Editor in Chief of The Atlantic as they unpack the past and imagine the American Jewish future.

 

 

Jeffrey Goldberg is the editor in chief of The Atlantic, and is the moderator of Washington Week With The Atlantic on PBS. He joined The Atlantic in 2007 as a national correspondent and in 2016 was named editor in chief, the 15th person to serve as editor in The Atlantic’s 168-year history. During his editorship, The Atlantic has set new audience and subscription records, and won its first-ever Pulitzer Prizes. In 2022, 2023, and 2024, The Atlantic received the National Magazine Award for General Excellence from the American Society of Magazine Editors, the top award in the industry.

title.rendered: The End of the Post Holocaust Era

content.rendered:
The post Holocaust era was a time of historical Jewish revival and renewal defined by the establishment of the state of Israel and success for Jews throughout the world, especially in America. It was a time marked by security, influence, and optimism about Jewish continuity. October 7 brought an end to that era revealing deep cracks and vulnerabilities. It sparked a need to reassess Jewish safety, identity, and peoplehood.  Join Yossi Klein Halevi as he unpacks what characterized the post Holocaust era and what this shift means for today’s Jewish communities locally and beyond.

title.rendered: Aspirational Zionism

content.rendered:
Join us to hear Yehuda Kurtzer, President of the Shalom Hartman Institute, as he shares reflections on what it means to embrace an aspirational Zionism today—one proudly committed to the Jewish people and responsive to the moral, spiritual, and political challenges of our time.

Following his remarks, Yehuda will be joined by Rabbi Yael Splansky of Holy Blossom for a conversation about how we can contribute to ensuring that Israel lives up to our deepest hopes and our highest values.
